title: The longest word there was

prereqs.why: Words are read into a `std::string` and compared by length.
The words keep coming until the input runs out, which is the same read-as-condition idiom as for numbers.

statement:
Read whitespace-separated words until the input runs out, then
print how many there were, the longest one, and how many characters
it has.

```
input:   the quick brown elephant ran

output:  words 5
         longest elephant
         letters 8
```

If two words are the longest, report the **first** of them.

If there are no words at all:

```
words 0
longest none
letters 0
```

### The point of the problem

`>>` on a `std::string` reads one whitespace-separated word, which
makes splitting a stream into words free:

```cpp
std::string word{};
while (std::cin >> word)
{
    // word holds the next one
}
```

It skips leading whitespace, reads until the next whitespace, and
does not care whether that whitespace is a space, a tab or a
newline. A line with three spaces between two words still yields
two words.

`word.size()` is its length. Keeping the longest so far is the same
running-maximum pattern as for numbers — with the same question
about what to start it at, and the same answer: the empty string
has length 0, so an empty `std::string` is a safe starting point
and **every** word beats it.

That only works because the strict comparison `>` keeps the first of
equals. Using `>=` would keep the last, which is a different answer
to the question that was asked.

### Constraints

Each word is at most 40 characters and there are at most 1000 of
them. Words may contain any printable characters other than
whitespace, including punctuation — `don’t` is one word and so is
`hello,`.

### Boundary cases

- **No input at all**, or input that is only whitespace: the three
  lines above.
- **One word** is both the count and the longest.
- **A tie**, as in `cat dog`, reports `cat` — which is what `>`
  rather than `>=` gives you.
- **Words spread over several lines** are no different from words on
  one line.
hints: The loop is `while (std::cin >> word)`. A `std::string` read with `>>` is one word, so the splitting is done for you.
Keep the best word so far in a `std::string` that starts empty. Every real word is longer than the empty string, so no special case for the first one is needed.
Compare with `>` and not `>=`, or a later word of the same length will replace the one you should have kept. `cat dog` must report `cat`.
